title: Indians in Dubai Face Job Losses and Pay Cuts as Iran War Hammers Gulf Economy
excerpt: <pThe ongoing conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran has sent shockwaves through the Gulf economy, and millions of Indian expatriates working in Dubai and across the UAE are bearing the brunt of the fall…
body:
The ongoing conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran has sent shockwaves through the Gulf economy, and millions of Indian expatriates working in Dubai and across the UAE are bearing the brunt of the fallout. With tourism drying up, construction projects stalling, and businesses shifting into what analysts call "survival mode," Indian workers in the region face an uncertain future.

Tourism Collapse and Business Slowdown

The International Monetary Fund has slashed its projection of the UAE's economic growth this year to just 3 percent — half of what it was in 2025. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz since the initial US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February has driven up the cost of energy, raw materials, and other production inputs, squeezing businesses across every sector.

Dubai's once-thriving tourism industry has taken a severe hit. Many of the city's wealthy visitors and residents have left, while new arrivals have all but stopped. Hotels, restaurants, and retail outlets that relied heavily on international tourism are cutting hours, reducing wages, and laying off staff. A Filipino sales supervisor told NPR that her company cut her hours in half after sales plummeted, forcing her to take a second job as a cleaner.

Indian Workers Hit Hardest

India is the largest source of migrant workers in the Gulf region, with an estimated 3.5 million Indians living in the UAE alone. Many work in construction, hospitality, retail, and logistics — sectors that have been devastated by the economic downturn. Reports from the Business and Human Rights Centre document widespread wage theft, layoffs, and unsafe working conditions affecting South Asian migrant workers since the conflict escalated.

The UAE's new localization mandate, which requires private firms to employ one Emirati for every foreigner on government-linked work, is compounding the pressure. Welding crews, riggers, and pipeline specialists — traditionally 90 to 95 percent expatriates — cannot be quickly replaced with local hires, but the mandate is pushing labour costs higher and slowing mobilization, according to industry experts quoted by Engineering News-Record.

Indian Firms Pivot to Survival

Major Indian companies with Gulf operations have scrambled to respond. Tata Consultancy Services activated its emergency call tree and said HR teams were "actively connected with associates and their families." Afcons Infrastructure, the flagship engineering arm of the Shapoorji Pallonji Group, had already reduced its manpower presence in the region as a precaution. EMA Partners India, which runs executive search operations from Dubai, asked its team to follow local safety protocols.

Meanwhile, recruitment pipelines from India to the Gulf have frozen. Kapil Gupta of Shella Consultants told Mint that about 80 workers headed for Bahrain and Qatar were halted, along with other regional recruitments.

A Silver Lining for Indian Contractors

Paradoxically, the reconstruction demand that will eventually follow the conflict could benefit India. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, and Bahrain are already tapping additional capacity from India, South Korea, and China. Several listed Indian government contractors are eyeing Middle East projects. But for the millions of Indian workers currently stuck in the Gulf with shrinking paychecks and rising living costs, that future remains distant.

On Dalal Street, Indian markets reflected the anxiety. The Nifty 50 was essentially flat on Thursday, with traders waiting for clarity on how the Middle East conflict evolves before taking aggressive positions.
author: Diaspora Desk
